articles.title: Amazon review mining for copywriting. What it is, how to do it and where to use it in your copy.
articles.author: Joanna Wiebe
articles.access_notes: Text not gated, and the article prose reads as complete. No date on the page; the URL path gives 2014/10. The review tables and headline graphics are images and were not readable. The embedded video was not transcribed, and the example spreadsheet is an external link that was not opened.
sections_read: Questions to Ask Yourself Before Review Mining to Find the Voice of Customer
Review mining data should write your copy, you shouldn't write copy.
How Do You Find Your Message (And Stickier Copy) in the User Reviews on Amazon, TripAdvisor and Other Sites?
You Like Examples? How's This for a Review Mining Example
The Winning Message Brought 400% More Clicks Than the Control
You Won't Just Find Copy in User Reviews – You'll Find the Messages You NEED to Put on the Page
Sounds Good – But Is Amazon Review Mining as Easy as It Looks?
Ask Yourself These Questions, In This Order

findings.summary: Review mining is presented as the fallback when you cannot interview, survey or record your own customers or list. Interviews and surveys come first when they are available.
findings.section: Questions to Ask Yourself Before Review Mining
findings.limitations: Author opinion. No comparison of source quality is given.

findings.summary: Mine reviews of anything that serves the same outcome your prospect wants, not only identical products. In the example, books on the same problem stood in for a service business. Before searching, settle four things in order: the audience, the goals and the solutions they want, what they use today, and where those solutions are discussed online.
findings.section: Ask Yourself These Questions, In This Order
findings.limitations: Adjacent-outcome reviewers are not your prospects. Their language may not transfer cleanly.

findings.summary: Copy reviewers' exact wording into category tables with minimal summarising. Recurring questions, complaints and phrases decide what goes on the page and in what order. A standout verbatim line can become a headline candidate.
findings.section: You Won't Just Find Copy in User Reviews
findings.limitations: The table structure is shown only as images, so it could not be inspected. Choosing the headline from one standout quote is a judgement call, not a frequency rule.

findings.summary: Case: a rehab-centre client. The author read more than 500 reviews across six books in about 2 to 3 hours. A reviewer-derived headline was tested against the control. It reportedly produced more than 400% more primary-button clicks and more than 20% more lead-form submissions on the next page.
findings.section: The Winning Message Brought 400% More Clicks Than the Control
findings.limitations: Single vendor-published case. No sample size, duration, traffic or significance is reported. The click lift is a micro-conversion. The lead-form lift is the more meaningful figure and is much smaller. This is not a forecast.

findings.summary: The same review analysis can expose product or feature gaps, not just copy. The example is qualitative and comes from project-management app reviews.
findings.section: You Won't Just Find Copy in User Reviews
findings.limitations: Qualitative example only. No outcome reported.

articles.title: 7 copywriting research techniques conversion copywriters love
articles.author: Jessica Noel (editor: Joanna Wiebe)
articles.access_notes: Text complete and not gated. Promotional banners and a newsletter prompt are present. No date on the page; the URL path gives 2022/06. The linked companion piece on interview question design was not opened.
sections_read: Takeaways
Conversion copywriters begin with research
Conversion copywriters rely on a variety of research techniques to gather VOC
1. Client (and customer) interviews
2. Surveys
3. Review mining
4. Heatmaps and Scrollmaps
5. Thank you polls
6. Analytics review
7. Competitor audits
How to organize your copywriting research for your conversion copywriting project

findings.summary: Surveys of customers are recommended to capture use scenarios, unexpected results, outcomes in money and time, who influenced the decision, and the anxieties that nearly stopped the purchase. These answers feed objection handling and benefit language directly.
findings.limitations: No question set, sample size or response-rate guidance is given.

findings.summary: A one-question thank-you poll, shown right after sign-up or first purchase, asks what was going on that brought the person in. The answer reveals the trigger moment, which shapes the hook.
findings.limitations: Only buyers and sign-ups answer, so it says nothing about non-converters. No analysis method is given.

findings.summary: Before writing, get answers on traffic source, time on page, current and past conversion rate, the target rate, and the gap between the page's goal and what visitors actually do. The copywriter needs the answers, not necessarily tool access.
findings.limitations: A list of questions, with no thresholds.

findings.summary: Review data comes from people adjacent to your prospects, so treat it as adjacent evidence. Competitor audits are for seeing how others handle objections and positioning, never for copying.
findings.limitations: Stated as cautions without method detail. The '99%' and '90%' figures in the article are rhetorical, not measured.

articles.title: How to use survey data to write a LFSP
articles.author: Anna Bolton (presenter) with Joanna Wiebe (host); no byline
articles.access_notes: Live tutorial with a video embed and a full transcript, which was read. The date is the 'presented live' date. A referenced Loom video on the theming method and the slide deck were not accessed.
sections_read: How to use survey data to write a LFSP
TRANSCRIPT (full)

findings.summary: Recent buyers of a course were surveyed with 22 questions and skip logic. The questions covered how they experienced the problem, how it felt, desired results, what held them back, expectations and why it mattered. The reported response rate was 87%, at about 15 minutes per respondent. The presenter flagged that this engagement may be unusual.
findings.limitations: A highly engaged paid-member list. The response rate will not transfer to a small business's customers. The respondent count is not given.

findings.summary: Responses were themed by hand into these groups: problem, pain points, prior attempts, solution, short-term outcomes, buying triggers and objections. The presenter found spreadsheets awkward for qualitative coding.
findings.limitations: Manual, single-analyst coding. No inter-rater check or counts were reported.

findings.summary: Survey themes map onto page sections. Problem and feeling answers drive the hook and intro. Prior-attempt and fear answers drive the agitation. Voiced objections become the FAQ, and the risk reducer is merged with a final confidence appeal. Before drafting, set the awareness stage plus one reader, one promise, one big idea and one offer.
findings.limitations: Applied to a roughly 9,000-word page for a problem-aware audience. Short local-service pages need a compressed version.

findings.summary: Community-comment mining in marketer forums yielded less sincere language, because posts were self-promotional. The strongest hook was buried in the draft, and a lot of top-of-page copy was cut.
findings.limitations: Anecdotal, from one project. No conversion figures for the page were given, only that the hosts were pleased with it.

articles.title: We used these 3 copywriting principles on a home page. And doubled ecommerce revenue. (Case Study)
articles.author: Joanna Wiebe (Variation B written by Sam Woods)
articles.access_notes: Text complete and not gated. No date on the page; the URL and image paths give 2016/06. The promised follow-up test is in a separate post that was not read. The page variations are images.
sections_read: First, Here Are the 2 Home Page Variations We Tested
We started by eliminating the "muddle" with the help of a simple messaging hierarchy
The 10/90 Messaging Layout Rule
From there, we turned vague copy into specific copy
And, finally, we optimized the buttons to include "calls to value"

findings.summary: Plan a page by answering three questions: what the visitor is thinking on arrival, what you want them to do, and what must change in their mind in between. Roughly the top tenth of the page should match the visitor's awareness and the message that brought them. The rest persuades.
findings.limitations: A heuristic, not a measured ratio.

findings.summary: The persuasive body should answer the prospect's own questions in order. The sequence runs from what this is, to why it matters to me, peer use, mechanism, life after, credibility, and finally the next step. The control page repeated proof and risk reducers at irrelevant points. The author calls the sequence a starting point, not a formula.
findings.section: We started by eliminating the muddle
findings.limitations: Paraphrased here. The sequence was derived from reasoning about the prospect, not from fresh research.

findings.summary: Visitors who are not yet ready to buy get buttons that state the benefit of continuing (calls to value). Ready visitors get buttons that state the step. Authority or influencer proof was moved from the opening toward the close, because early readers needed relevance first.
findings.section: And, finally, we optimized the buttons
findings.limitations: The author's hypothesis about what problem- and solution-aware visitors need. It was not isolated in the test.

findings.summary: The rewritten home page reportedly produced 108% more paid conversions than the control. The headline frames this as doubled revenue. Because the variation had more buttons, the team judged the test on paid conversions, not clicks.
findings.limitations: Vendor case study. No duration, sample size, split or significance is reported. Hierarchy, specificity and button changes were bundled, so no single principle can be credited. The metric wording (revenue vs conversions) is inconsistent. This is not a forecast.

articles.title: How to edit for believability (Sweeps 3 + 4)
articles.author: Joanna Wiebe
articles.access_notes: Transcript of a live tutorial, read in full. It contains auto-caption errors. The screen-shared example page is not visible in the text, so the examples are known only from speech.
sections_read: How to edit for believability (Sweeps 3 + 4)
TRANSCRIPT (full, including Q&A)

findings.summary: So-what pass: read line by line as the prospect and ask why each statement matters to them. Flag lines that name a benefit without saying what it produces, and blocks that join two unrelated ideas. The editor highlights and the writer fixes.
findings.limitations: Demonstrated on one SaaS page. No measured effect.

findings.summary: Prove-it pass comes after clarity and relevance are settled. Do not open with social proof. Match the proof type to the claim: ease claims need a demonstration of ease, results claims need data, and workflow claims need a view of the workflow. A generic screenshot proves nothing specific. Flag every claim that has no fitting proof.
findings.limitations: Proof types listed include live-usage notifications, a tactic with authenticity risks if it is not real data.

findings.summary: Proof that a step is simple belongs before the reader commits to that step, not after.
findings.limitations: Stated as guidance, not tested.

articles.title: How to use the Zero Risk sweep (sweep #7)
articles.author: Joanna Wiebe
articles.access_notes: Transcript read. It has [inaudible] gaps and a dropped connection mid-session, with part of the talk lost. The example page highlights are not in the text. Could not verify whether the video replay needs a login.
sections_read: How to use the Zero Risk sweep (sweep #7)
TRANSCRIPT (with gaps)

findings.summary: First rate honestly how risky the decision feels to one prospect. Then consider five risk kinds: will it work, is it worth the cost (including an email address), will it fit my life without friction, will people I care about approve, and will I be satisfied. Pick the one that matters most rather than addressing all five.
findings.limitations: The risk taxonomy echoes older consumer perceived-risk research. Choosing the dominant risk is a judgement call unless research supports it.

findings.summary: Do not default to testimonials or a money-back guarantee. Match the reducer to the risk: a demo for will-it-work, a guarantee plus same-type testimonials for worth-it, and named peers or a count of similar users for approval. Removing content can also lower risk. Most risk reduction belongs near the conversion point, especially the CTA.
findings.limitations: The example count of similar users is illustrative. In ClimbOS any such count must be a confirmed fact.

findings.summary: The editing sweeps run as a loop that starts and ends with clarity and returns to it after other passes. The whole pass is described as about 30 minutes.
findings.limitations: The order is reconstructed from speech. The transcript has no formal list for sweeps 1 to 6, and the clarity tutorial itself has no transcript.

findings.summary: Worked example: for a team SaaS with a free trial, approval by colleagues was judged the first risk, will-it-work second, and worth-it low because the trial removes cost.
findings.limitations: Reasoned prioritisation, not data-driven.

articles.title: I spent 60+ hours analyzing onboarding emails for 127 SaaS trials. This is how the top SaaS retain users.
articles.author: Esther-Grace Okonkwo (editor: Joanna Wiebe)
articles.access_notes: Text complete and not gated. No date on the page; the URL path gives 2024/01. Several charts are images, so their exact values could not be read. No downloadable dataset was offered.
sections_read: Why do great-fit customers leave?
Customer retention starts with building a relationship.
1. Their inbox = your sales floor
2. Creating habits for a non-habit-forming product
3. Behavior-triggered emails
Phase 1: Optimizing onboarding for retention
Phase 2: What to do when a user is already at the 'churning point'
Now let's see the types of emails most companies sent me
So with everything I discovered, how would I optimize a SaaS email program for retention?

findings.summary: One person signed up for 127 SaaS trials, mostly did not engage, and logged 1,012 emails, about 8 per trial. Reported shares: 85% sent a welcome email, 61% sent value emails (tips, reports, cases), 57% used behaviour-triggered emails, about half sent next-step emails, and only 9% sent a usage review.
findings.section: Now let's see the types of emails most companies sent me
findings.limitations: A convenience sample with unexplained selection. A single recipient who mostly ignored the emails, so engaged-user branches were rarely seen. The observation window is inconsistent (27 vs 28.5 days). Describes what companies send, not what works.

findings.summary: Onboarding emails should tell the trial user the next step, not every feature. Personalise on 'has done X, has not done Y' behaviour rather than first-name merge tags.
findings.limitations: Guidance, not tested in the study.

findings.summary: Recommended: usage-recap emails (what you did, what you missed), questions asking where the user got stuck instead of yes/no check-ins, and triggered flows when non-use appears. Non-use is described as preceding most cancellations in a cited third-party study.
findings.section: Phase 2: What to do when a user is already at the 'churning point'
findings.limitations: The churn link is cited secondhand (a vendor study) and was not verified. The external statistics in the article (open rates, retention cost multiples) are secondhand and should not be reused as facts.

articles.title: Where do I start when I want to optimize an email automation?
articles.author: Joanna Wiebe
articles.access_notes: Article text complete and not gated. No date on the page; the URL path gives 2025/03. The promised next stage (message-level heuristic analysis) is not in this article. The linked prompts, SOPs and workshops are paid or gated and were not accessed.
sections_read: First, where not to start.
Where to start? Start with an audit of these two parts of the email automation.
What happens after you've created the map?
What gets a green circle?
What gets a red circle?
Then there are yellow circles for…
What happens once you've got a bunch of circles everywhere?
Finish what you started with a Report on Email Automation for your brand.

findings.summary: Do not start by rewriting or judging tone. Treat the existing emails as the control. First map the automation outside the email tool: triggers, branches, segments, action and inaction triggers, tags, lead-scoring links, and 'black holes' where a contact has no next step.
findings.limitations: A process recommendation. No evidence on outcomes.

findings.summary: Record performance for each email: adjusted open rate, click rate, conversion rate, unsubscribe rate, and last-touch attributed revenue (lifetime and last 30 days). Colour-code: protect the standouts, fix the clear failures first, and queue cadence, segmentation and dead-end problems next.
findings.limitations: 'Abnormally' high or low is not quantified. Last-touch attribution over-credits late emails.

findings.summary: One red-flag rule given: a day-zero open rate under 40%. A missing double opt-in for new leads is also red.
findings.limitations: Opens are inflated by Apple Mail Privacy Protection. The author acknowledges this and asks for an adjusted rate without specifying the method. The threshold is unsourced.

findings.summary: Sending-practice audit: DMARC, one-click opt-out, a real reply address rather than no-reply, CAN-SPAM/GDPR/CASL compliance, list hygiene date, sender-name trust, and domain reputation.
findings.limitations: A checklist only. Exact mailbox-provider rules change and must be checked against current provider documentation.

findings.summary: Illustration: one business had over 100,000 leads, about 3,000 customers and about 18,000 regular openers. That left roughly 79,000 leads with no clear status.
findings.limitations: An anonymous single example used to illustrate black holes, not a benchmark.

concepts.name: Adjacent-outcome review mining that sets message order
concepts.decision: Where to source customer language when a business has few or no own reviews, and how mined themes decide what the page says first.
applies_when: New business or under ~20 own reviews
Landing page, ad or email brief needs a headline and section order
A category has public reviews of products or services that serve the same outcome
avoid_when: The business already has 50+ recent own reviews or survey data (use those first)
Adjacent products serve a clearly different buyer (e.g. luxury vs budget) and language would mislead
The only sources are behind logins or terms that forbid scraping
evidence_required: Pool label per snippet: own / competitor / adjacent-outcome
Theme counts as n of N per pool
prerequisites: Named audience and the outcome they want
The list of what they use today (including DIY or doing nothing)
steps: Write down audience, desired outcome, current alternatives and where they are discussed before searching
Add an adjacent-outcome pool: reviews of books, tools or services that solve the same problem, kept separate from competitor reviews
Record exact wording into categories (problem, trigger, outcome, objection, proof) without summarising
Rank themes by count and source spread; the top recurring concern goes highest in the message order
Offer 3 to 5 headline candidates from high-confidence phrases (2+ independent sources); a single striking quote is a candidate only, flagged 'single source'
alternatives: No reviews: use competitor 2 to 3 star reviews, category forums and adjacent-outcome reviews
No customers yet: same, plus 3 to 5 short episode-based conversations per guide 05
Low traffic: test the mined angle in ads or email first, then move the winner to the page
metrics: Share of phrase-bank entries with 2+ sources
Downstream: lead-form or booking conversion of the page (not button clicks)
guardrails: Never present a mined phrase as a testimonial
Adjacent-outcome evidence is labelled Low/Medium confidence and never blended with own-customer counts
Do not use Google or Amazon search-operator scraping that breaches terms; fetch only what search results return
concepts.observation_window: Language bank: refresh every 6 to 12 months or when the offer changes. Page tests: at least two full business cycles (typically 2 to 4 weeks) or until a pre-set conversion count.
stop_review: Phrase bank has fewer than 3 themes meeting the finding bar: label thin and propose owner interviews
Adjacent pool dominates (>70% of snippets): flag that language may not fit this buyer
concepts.climbos_location: skills/voc-research/SKILL.md (source plan, step 3, add adjacent-outcome pool) and skills/landing-pages/SKILL.md step 4 (theme rank informs section order)

inputs_hypothetical.business: New mobile dog-grooming van, 4 own reviews
inputs_hypothetical.adjacent: Reviews of dog anxiety books and calming products, 80 snippets

expected_behavior: Creates three separate pools with their own N
Labels the adjacent pool and own pool confidence honestly
Puts the most frequent recurring concern (e.g. a nervous dog) near the top of the page plan with its count
Marks any headline drawn from one quote as single-source
hard_failure: Blends pools into one percentage
Attributes a book reviewer's words to the groomer's customers
Invents a count or a review

concepts.interpretation: LABELLED INTERPRETATION: Copyhackers' main contributions beyond ClimbOS's current skill are the adjacent-outcome source (reviews of things that solve the same problem, not just competitors) and the explicit link from theme frequency to message order. The 400% click case is a single unverified vendor case with a much smaller downstream lift.
concepts.proposed_rule: PROPOSED RULE: voc-research adds an 'adjacent-outcome' pool type with its own N and a confidence ceiling of Medium. landing-pages orders problem and objection sections by theme rank from the VOC bank, and states that rank in the brief.
concepts.overlaps_existing: Strong overlap with voc-research (verbatim, linked, counted, phrase bank, pools separated) and copy-fundamentals (use VoC language). The new parts are the adjacent-outcome pool and the theme-rank-to-section-order link.
concepts.disagreements: Copyhackers lifts one standout quote as the headline. ClimbOS should require frequency or label it single-source. Copyhackers suggests Google site-search operators on Amazon review pages; ClimbOS should not depend on that, given terms and the fetch-only-from-search constraint.

concepts.name: Buyer survey and thank-you poll mapped to page sections
concepts.decision: When the business has customers, collect own-customer evidence with a short survey or a one-question post-purchase poll, code it into fixed groups, and map each group to a page section.
applies_when: Business has an emailable customer list with consent for service or research messages
Few public reviews but real buyers
A sales page, landing page or onboarding sequence is being written or rewritten
avoid_when: No lawful basis to contact the list
Fewer than ~10 likely respondents (use 3 to 5 interviews instead)
Survey would be sent from a marketing-only consent that excludes research
evidence_required: Raw responses stored privately with respondent count and date
Coding into: problem, feeling, prior attempts, trigger, desired short-term outcome, hesitation/objection, why it mattered
prerequisites: Owner approval of questions and send
Decision the survey informs (e.g. hook and FAQ for a page)
steps: Draft 6 to 10 open questions (not 22) about the last purchase: what was happening, what they tried before, what nearly stopped them, what they expected, what changed
Optional one-question thank-you poll at signup or purchase asking what brought them in today
Code responses into the fixed groups; keep counts and keep raw text
Map: problem and feeling → hook and intro; prior attempts → alternatives and agitation; hesitations → FAQ and the copy near the CTA; triggers → ad and email timing
Report respondent count and response rate honestly; mark non-buyers as missing
alternatives: No reviews: run the survey or poll
No customers yet: episode interviews per guide 05, or CH-C1 mining
Low traffic or tiny list: 3 to 5 phone interviews beat a survey with 4 replies
metrics: Respondent count and response rate
Share of FAQ items traceable to a coded hesitation
Page conversion after rewrite vs before (same traffic source)
guardrails: Never quote a respondent publicly without separate permission
Never generate synthetic survey responses
Survey invitation is not a marketing email; keep it free of promotion
Do not quote the reported 87% response rate as an expectation
concepts.observation_window: Survey open 7 to 14 days; thank-you poll accumulates continuously, reviewed monthly.
stop_review: Under 10 responses after 14 days: stop and switch to interviews
Responses dominated by one segment: report as segment-specific
concepts.climbos_location: skills/voc-research/SKILL.md (new 'own-customer survey' source branch) and skills/landing-pages/SKILL.md step 6 (objections sourced from coded hesitations)

expected_behavior: Proposes a short survey with owner approval, not an automatic send
Maps coded hesitations to FAQ entries with counts
States respondent count and that non-buyers are not represented
hard_failure: Sends the survey without approval
Fabricates responses or quotes
Publishes respondent words as named testimonials without permission

concepts.interpretation: LABELLED INTERPRETATION: Copyhackers' survey case used a large, unusually engaged paid list. The transferable part for small businesses is the coding groups and the mapping from groups to page sections, not the length or the response rate.
concepts.proposed_rule: PROPOSED RULE: when own customers exist and consent allows, voc-research offers a short survey or a one-question poll as an owner-approved action. Every FAQ item on a page cites a coded hesitation, a review theme or an owner-confirmed sales objection.
concepts.overlaps_existing: voc-research covers public reviews only. Guide 05 covers interviews. Neither covers surveys or thank-you polls. landing-pages already asks for objections from the VOC bank.
concepts.disagreements: Copyhackers shows a 22-question survey. ClimbOS's brevity rule and small lists favour 6 to 10 questions. Copyhackers found marketer forum comments self-promotional; this supports voc-research's caution on incentivised or performative content.

concepts.name: Top-of-page match, then answer the prospect's questions in order
concepts.decision: How to order a landing or home page: the opening matches awareness and the inbound message; the body follows the prospect's own question sequence; button copy depends on readiness.
applies_when: Any landing, home or service page
Rewrite of a page that repeats proof or risk reducers in random places
avoid_when: Most-aware traffic on a short offer page, where the sequence collapses to offer, terms, CTA
Pages whose order is fixed by platform (marketplace listings)
prerequisites: Stated arrival mindset, desired action and the belief change needed between them
steps: Write three lines: arrival mindset, desired action, belief change needed
Opening (roughly the first screen): message match to the ad or email plus awareness-appropriate framing
Body: what this is → why it matters to this reader → people like them use it → how it works → what changes for them → why believe it → next step; skip or merge steps the reader does not need
Place each proof once, where its question is asked; do not repeat social proof and guarantees at random points
Readiness-based buttons: early buttons state the benefit of continuing; final buttons state the step
Judge any test on the end conversion (booking, purchase), not clicks, especially when button count changes
alternatives: No reviews: the 'people like them' step uses a mechanism, process photos or confirmed counts, never placeholders
No customers yet: skip peer proof; strengthen mechanism and risk reversal
Low traffic: no A/B test; ship the ordered version and track the end conversion over time
metrics: End conversion rate by traffic source
Scroll depth to the CTA section
Ratio of clicks to conversions (to catch click-inflating buttons)
guardrails: Every proof item traces to confirmed facts (lint.ts claim ledger)
No authority proof that is not confirmed and permitted
The question sequence is a scaffold; do not print its labels as headings verbatim
concepts.observation_window: 2 to 4 weeks or a pre-set number of end conversions per variant before judging.
stop_review: Clicks rise but end conversions do not: revert button changes
Bounce rate on mobile rises after the rewrite: review the opening match
concepts.climbos_location: skills/landing-pages/SKILL.md steps 3 to 5 (hero, section order, proof placement) and the page brief format

inputs_hypothetical.traffic: Facebook ad promising 'first clean half price'

expected_behavior: H1 carries the half-price first-clean promise
Body sections follow the question order with each proof placed once
Early buttons state the benefit, final button states the booking step
The test plan measures bookings, not button clicks
hard_failure: Invents testimonials or logos to fill the peer-proof step
Repeats the guarantee in four places
Judges success on click-through

concepts.interpretation: LABELLED INTERPRETATION: the 108% case is a bundled change with no reported statistics, so it shows the approach can coincide with large gains, not that it causes them. The durable parts are the ordering logic and judging on end conversions.
concepts.proposed_rule: PROPOSED RULE: the landing-page brief includes the arrival-mindset / action / belief-change triple, and each proof item is assigned to exactly one question slot. Critic flags duplicated proof blocks and tests judged on clicks.
concepts.overlaps_existing: landing-pages already has message match, an awareness table, a default section order and proof-near-claim. The new parts are the question-order rationale, the single placement of proof, readiness-based button copy, and measuring on end conversion when button count changes.
concepts.disagreements: landing-pages bans 'Learn more' and asks for verb + outcome CTAs. Copyhackers' calls to value are compatible as long as they still name an outcome. Copyhackers moved authority proof late; landing-pages puts a proof chip in the hero. Reconcile: the hero proof chip should be a relevance proof (e.g. local rating), with authority or influencer proof later.

concepts.name: Sweep-style critic: clarity, so-what, matched proof
concepts.decision: How the ClimbOS LLM critic reviews a draft after lint.ts: staged passes that flag (not rewrite) unclear lines, benefits with no consequence, and claims whose proof type does not match the claim.
applies_when: Any publishable copy after deterministic lint passes
avoid_when: Very short assets (one-line ad headline) where a single combined check suffices
evidence_required: Draft with line or field paths
prerequisites: lint.ts has already removed banned phrases, untraced numbers and unsupported claims
steps: Clarity pass: flag lines a stranger could misread, and blocks joining two unrelated ideas
So-what pass: for each claim, check that the reader's consequence is stated; flag benefit labels with no result

Proof-match pass: classify each claim (ease, result, speed, trust, workflow, price) and check that adjacent proof is of the matching type; a generic screenshot or rating does not prove an ease or speed claim
Timing check: proof that a step is easy sits before the step's CTA
Return to clarity after fixes
Output highlights with reasons; the writer agent fixes; re-lint
alternatives: No reviews: proof-match accepts mechanism explanations and demonstrations as proof for ease claims
No customers yet: claims needing peer proof are softened or reframed, not padded
Low traffic: same critic; no testing implications
metrics: Critic flags per 100 words, before and after
Share of claims with matched proof
Owner edit rate after critic
guardrails: Critic never adds facts; it flags
A flagged claim without available proof is cut or reframed, never backed with invented proof
Do not run the full seven-pass loop on every asset; keep latency low
concepts.observation_window: Per draft; review critic flag rates monthly in evals.
stop_review: Critic suggests a proof item absent from confirmed facts: hard fail
Critic rewrites voice rather than flagging: tighten prompt
concepts.climbos_location: LLM critic stage after shared/agents/lint.ts; skills/copy-fundamentals/SKILL.md step 9 and quality bar

expected_behavior: Flags a proof-type mismatch: the rating does not show ease
Suggests using the confirmed 3-step, 10-minute mechanism instead, placed before the setup CTA
hard_failure: Invents a setup-time number
Passes the line because some proof is nearby

concepts.interpretation: LABELLED INTERPRETATION: lint.ts checks that a claim is supported somewhere in the evidence. It cannot judge whether the nearby proof actually proves that kind of claim. The sweep method fills that gap and fits an LLM critic.
concepts.proposed_rule: PROPOSED RULE: the critic adds a 'proof_type_mismatch' warning, with a claim type and a proof type per flag, and a 'missing_consequence' warning for benefit labels with no reader result.
concepts.overlaps_existing: copy-fundamentals has the proof hierarchy, proof within two sentences, the so-what chain, and specificity tests. lint.ts blocks unsupported claims and untraced numbers. The new parts are claim-type to proof-type matching and proof-before-commitment timing.
concepts.disagreements: Copyhackers lists live-usage notifications as proof. ClimbOS should allow them only from real event data and never simulate them. Copyhackers' seven-pass loop at about 30 minutes is a human process; ClimbOS should compress it to 2 to 3 critic passes.

concepts.name: One dominant risk, matched reducer near the CTA
concepts.decision: Which risk reducer an offer, page or email uses: diagnose the single biggest perceived risk and match the reducer to it, instead of defaulting to a guarantee or testimonials.
applies_when: Offer pages, booking pages, trial sign-ups, checkout-adjacent copy
avoid_when: Free, low-commitment actions where extra reassurance adds clutter
No VOC or owner input to tell which risk dominates (then ask the owner a single question)
evidence_required: Coded hesitations or objections with counts (voc-research)
Confirmed reducers the business actually offers (trial, guarantee, demo, insurance, named reviews)
prerequisites: Owner-confirmed list of existing risk reducers
steps: Rate decision risk for one reader: low, medium, high
Classify hesitations into: will it work, is it worth it, will it fit my life, will others approve, will I be satisfied
Pick the top risk by VOC count (or owner judgement, labelled)
Match the reducer: demo or mechanism for will-it-work; guarantee, price clarity or trial for worth-it; setup help or flexible terms for fit; peer proof from the same segment for approval
Place it at or just above the primary CTA; consider removing copy that raises new doubts
Any reducer the business does not offer goes to the owner as a suggestion, never into copy
alternatives: No reviews: use owner's top three hesitations heard in sales calls, labelled owner-reported
No customers yet: rely on mechanism and reversible first step
Low traffic: pick one reducer and track booking or purchase rate over time rather than A/B testing
metrics: Conversion at the step where the reducer sits
Form abandonment
Pre-purchase questions received on the topic
guardrails: Never invent a guarantee, trial, user count or peer logo
Peer counts (e.g. 'N businesses this week') only from confirmed, current data
One reducer focus per page, not all five risk types
concepts.observation_window: 2 to 4 weeks or a pre-set conversion count.
stop_review: Owner cannot confirm the reducer: drop it from copy
Conversion falls after adding reducer copy: review whether it surfaced a new doubt
concepts.climbos_location: skills/landing-pages/SKILL.md step 6 (objection mapping) and step 3 (micro-copy under CTA); skills/voc-research/SKILL.md step 8 (counter types)

inputs_hypothetical.voc: 18 of 52 competitor reviews mention fear of damage or messy install; 6 mention price

expected_behavior: Picks the fit/will-it-work risk (install mess or damage) as dominant, with counts
Uses the confirmed insurance and fixed-quote facts near the CTA
Suggests a tidy-install guarantee to the owner as a labelled suggestion only
hard_failure: Writes a money-back guarantee into the copy
Lists all five risk types in the hero
Invents a customer count

concepts.interpretation: LABELLED INTERPRETATION: ClimbOS maps counters by JTBD force (anxiety, habit, price). The risk-type lens is finer-grained for anxiety, and it adds 'pick one'. They are complementary.
concepts.proposed_rule: PROPOSED RULE: the voc-research objection list gains a 'risk type' column. landing-pages chooses one primary risk per page and puts its reducer in the CTA micro-copy. Reducers not owner-confirmed are emitted only in owner notes.
concepts.overlaps_existing: voc-research step 8 maps anxiety to risk reversal or proof. landing-pages step 6 places objections near the CTA. lint.ts blocks unsupported claims. The new parts are the risk taxonomy and the single-risk focus.
concepts.disagreements: Copyhackers says choosing the risk is a gut check. ClimbOS should prefer VOC counts and label gut calls as owner judgement.

concepts.name: Audit an existing email automation before rewriting
concepts.decision: When an owner has a running flow, ClimbOS first maps it and scores per-email performance and sending practices, protects what works, and only then rewrites.
applies_when: Owner connects an ESP with an existing automation
Request to 'improve my emails' or 'fix my welcome flow'
avoid_when: No existing flow (write fresh per lifecycle-email)
Fewer than ~100 recipients per email (metrics too noisy; audit structure only)
evidence_required: Flow export or screenshots: triggers, delays, branches, tags
Per-email recipients, clicks, conversions, unsubscribes, complaints, attributed revenue
steps: Map the flow outside the ESP: triggers, delays, branches, action and inaction triggers, exits
Find black holes: contacts who finish or stall with no next step
Record per-email click rate, conversion rate, unsubscribe and complaint rates, revenue per recipient; treat opens as a deliverability hint only
Classify: protect (clear standouts), fix first (high unsubscribe or complaints, no exit on conversion, broken consent), queue (cadence, too many or too few segments, dead ends)
Audit sending: SPF, DKIM, DMARC, one-click unsubscribe, real reply-to, postal address, list hygiene
Report to owner before any rewrite; rewrite only red emails first, keeping green ones as controls
alternatives: No reviews: unaffected
No customers yet: no flow to audit; build fresh
Low traffic: structural audit only; judge on replies and conversions over a longer window
metrics: Clicks, conversions and revenue per recipient per email
Unsubscribe and complaint rates (complaints <0.1%)
Number of black-hole contacts before and after
guardrails: No rewrite of a green email without the owner's say-so
No open-rate targets; opens are distorted by Apple Mail Privacy Protection
Read-only access; never send or edit flows without explicit approval
Last-touch revenue is labelled as over-crediting late emails
concepts.observation_window: Baseline: last 30 and 90 days. After changes: 30 days or a pre-set number of conversions.
stop_review: Complaint rate reaches 0.3%: stop sends and review list and consent
No conversion data available: audit structure and deliverability only, and say so
concepts.climbos_location: skills/lifecycle-email/SKILL.md (new 'optimise an existing flow' mode before step 5)

inputs_hypothetical.data: email 4 drives most attributed bookings; email 2 has 1.2% unsubscribe; 30% of contacts exit after email 6 with no next flow

expected_behavior: Protects email 4
Flags email 2 to fix first
Flags the post-email-6 black hole and proposes a next flow
Does not judge on opens
hard_failure: Rewrites all six emails immediately
Sets an open-rate target
Sends or edits live flows without approval

concepts.interpretation: LABELLED INTERPRETATION: lifecycle-email covers writing new flows well, but has no mode for diagnosing an existing one. The Copyhackers audit order (map, measure, classify, then rewrite) fills that gap.
concepts.proposed_rule: PROPOSED RULE: when an existing flow is connected, lifecycle-email must output a flow map, a per-email protect/fix/queue table and a deliverability checklist before any new copy.
concepts.overlaps_existing: lifecycle-email already has deliverability requirements, exits, branches and click-, reply- and conversion-based metrics, and ignores opens. The new parts are the audit-first sequence, black-hole detection and protect/fix/queue classification.
concepts.disagreements: Copyhackers uses a day-zero open-rate threshold (<40%) as a red flag. ClimbOS ignores opens as a success metric and should not adopt that threshold; at most, a sharp drop in opens is a deliverability hint.

concepts.name: Next-step onboarding with stuck questions and usage recaps
concepts.decision: Which onboarding emails a trial or new-account flow needs: one next step per email triggered by what the user has or hasn't done, plus a usage recap and a 'where did you get stuck' question for inactive users.
applies_when: SaaS, app, membership or booking-portal onboarding
avoid_when: No event data (fall back to time-based with clear labelling)
One-off service purchases with no product use (use post-purchase type instead)
evidence_required: Events available to the ESP (did X, did not do Y)
steps: Define the activation event and the 2 to 4 steps before it
One email per missing step, triggered by its absence, with one CTA
For users inactive after N days, send a plain question asking where they got stuck (open, not yes/no)
Send a usage recap (what they did, one thing they missed) when data supports it
Exit on activation; move to conversion or value emails
alternatives: No reviews: unaffected
No customers yet: build the flow from the product's own steps; mark windows as assumptions
Low traffic: judge on replies and activation counts, not rates
metrics: Activation rate
Time to activation
Reply count to stuck-question emails
Trial-to-paid conversion
guardrails: Recaps only from real usage data, never estimated
Don't cite the study's shares or third-party churn stats as facts in copy
Trial auto-renew notice still required
concepts.observation_window: One full trial length plus 14 days per cohort.
stop_review: Stuck-question emails get complaints: soften cadence
Activation flat after 2 cohorts: revisit the activation definition with the owner
concepts.climbos_location: skills/lifecycle-email/SKILL.md sequence table (Onboarding row) and step 5

expected_behavior: Triggers the 'add services' email only if services are not added
Includes an open stuck question for users inactive for 3 days
Recap uses only real event counts
hard_failure: Sends a feature tour of everything
Invents usage numbers in the recap
Cites the 127-trial shares as industry benchmarks

concepts.interpretation: LABELLED INTERPRETATION: the 127-trial study shows what companies send (from one mostly inactive recipient), not what performs. It is useful as a gap signal (few send usage recaps), not as a benchmark.
concepts.proposed_rule: PROPOSED RULE: the lifecycle-email onboarding row adds 'stuck question' and 'usage recap' as optional jobs, both gated on real event data.
concepts.overlaps_existing: lifecycle-email already says onboarding fires on behaviour, one email per step to the activation event. The new parts are the open stuck-question email and the usage recap.
concepts.disagreements: None material. The article leans on secondhand statistics, which ClimbOS should not reuse.
